title: Choose Webshelf's visual world
question: Previews added for the roll, the pick and Midnight Line Map: each shows a desktop results page (a topic search) and a phone (a tool search). They are quick code sketches with sample results, not the final build. Every option keeps your four behaviours.

options.label: Genre Bands
options.lineage: Edward Young's 1935 three-band paperback covers, colour-coded by genre
options.thesis: Every results page is a paperback cover coded by genre: the band's colour tells you what kind of answer is waiting before you read a word. Your three books are the three genres.
materials: a white middle band for reading
your brown shelf as the rule between them
options.viewport: A full-width colour band holds your mark (recoloured where needed) and the search field; it sits on your brown shelf. The band takes the genre of the search: sky blue for web results, green when there's a topic panel, amber when a tool answers (calculator, weather, converter). In the mark, the book for that genre stands upright while the others lean. Below, the white reading band: results as a single scannable list, titles in a confident humanist sans, notes in a book serif, the topic panel at right on wide screens and after the first result on phones. A thin bottom band closes the page. Dark mode keeps the band colours and turns the reading band to ink-black.
options.risk: The three-band grid is famous; set too literally (Gill-alike caps, a cartouche, cover pastiche) it reads as homage costume. The build takes the grid and the genre code only, never the publisher's furniture.

raised.raise: Dark mode is a true negative: identical structure and spacing, only the values change.
Hierarchy rides one ramp, type size; no stacking of weight, colour and boxes to say the same thing.
The genre colour never decorates; only things you can press or that tell you the genre carry it, and every touch target is at least 44px.
The next results are already loaded before you reach the end of the list.

options.label: The First Web Page
options.lineage: the 1991 hypertext documents that started the web
options.thesis: Webshelf set like the first web: plain document type, underlined links, horizontal rules, and nothing that isn't text or a link.
options.viewport: Your lockup small at top left; the search field as a plain bordered input; results as a numbered list of underlined titles with the address beneath; rules separate sections.
options.risk: The most familiar card here: many 'old web' projects already use default-document styling, and it can read as unfinished rather than chosen.

options.label: Midnight Line Map
options.lineage: metropolitan rail maps fired in enamel
options.thesis: Your four book colours become four lines on a midnight ground; every search is a route, every kind of answer a line.
options.viewport: Midnight header with the search field; result kinds marked by coloured line bullets; the topic panel as an interchange circle where lines meet.
options.case: Holds on audience, because your four book colours map onto four lines almost exactly, but loses on clarity: a route map is a stretch for a list of results.
options.risk: Becomes a transit costume (stations, interchanges) the moment the metaphor goes past colour and line bullets.

options.label: Gridded Specimen
options.thesis: The web as a grid made visible: faint construction lines, monumental grid-built type on the homepage, neutral grotesk for everything you read.
options.viewport: A faint grid under the whole page; the query set large on the grid; results snapped to whole cells; your lockup placed on the grid like a specimen.
options.case: Holds on audience for design-literate people (you included) and on 'properly minimalist', but loses on clarity: a visible grid adds noise to a page people scan in seconds.
options.risk: The visible grid turns decorative fast; the detector flags decorative grid backgrounds.

options.label: Datamatics
options.case: Loses both axes: strobing data fields and monospace columns fight reading and say nothing about search.
options.kept: Dark mode as a true negative of the light theme.

options.label: Star Atlas
options.case: Loses both axes: dot-size hierarchy doesn't fit a list of links, and the night sky says nothing about the web.

options.label: Warm Consumer App
options.case: Loses both axes: it's the generic app default, and its warm ground is the reflexive beige.
options.kept: Colour only where something can be pressed; generous touch targets.

options.label: Vertical Feed
options.case: Loses both axes: one item per screen destroys the scannable list.
options.kept: The next thing is already loaded.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: What search engines ship, executed impeccably: white page, centred pill, blue links.
canonCard.viewport: The arrangement every visitor expects, at full craft.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from the competition by design; this is close to the version you called rubbish.
